criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Both sides are presented (three arguments each), but the 'for' arguments are speculative and shallow (e.g., the Apple analogy compares consumer phones to enterprise servers). Conclusions on decision-making focus on Rachel and her company; other stakeholders' decision-making is not separately addressed.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.

However, there is essentially no quantitative evidence (no failure rates, cost figures), and the BBC reference lacks a URL, so not Excellent.

overall: A well-structured, readable report with a clear 'not ship' position supported by relevant case studies (NHS, Volkswagen) and a code of ethics. Arguments are balanced but somewhat shallow, lack quantitative evidence, use no visual elements, and contain minor typos and incomplete references. All task requirements are addressed.

feedback.summary: You produced a well-structured, readable report that addresses all task requirements and argues a clear 'not ship' position. Your use of the NHS and Volkswagen case studies and the Engineers Australia Code of Ethics is a real strength. To reach the top band, deepen your arguments with quantitative evidence, analyse every stakeholder you identify, and add visual elements with polished referencing.
next_steps: Add quantitative evidence to the Discussion (e.g., defect/failure rates, recall or fine costs) so your risk and cost arguments rest on data, not speculation.
Analyse the 'chip contract company' stakeholder in the body, and add decision-making conclusions for other stakeholders (government health department, end-users), not just Rachel and her company.

Replace the Apple analogy with a safety-critical example, verify the Engineers Australia clause numbers you cite, fix typos ('DICUSSION', 'EACE'), and complete your IEEE references (add URL and access date for [3], full details for [1]).

criteria.C1: You clearly identify several ethical issues (public safety vs business pressure, professional integrity) and link them to engineering design and organisational context, with stakeholders explicitly listed in the Introduction. To reach Excellent, describe the significance of each issue in more depth, and ensure every stakeholder you list — including the chip contract company — is actually analysed later in the report.
criteria.C2: You present three arguments on each side, which shows balance, but the 'for' arguments are speculative and shallow — the Apple analogy compares consumer smartphones to safety-critical enterprise servers, which weakens the competitive-pressure point. Your conclusions focus only on Rachel and her company. Excellent requires objective arguments with significant depth and decision-making recommendations for several different stakeholders.
criteria.C3: Your body follows a logical for/against structure with linked paragraphs, and the NHS and Volkswagen cases compellingly support your 'not ship' conclusion — well done. To reach Excellent, extend this systematic understanding to all stakeholders: the chip contract company is listed in your Introduction but never discussed, which leaves your stakeholder coverage incomplete.
criteria.C4: Your four references, including two substantive external case studies (NHS IT failures, VW emissions) and the Engineers Australia Code of Ethics, provide good qualitative support. Excellent requires both qualitative and quantitative evidence: add figures such as defect or failure rates, or the financial scale of fines and recalls, to substantiate your risk and cost arguments. Also complete reference [3] with a URL and [1] with full details.
criteria.C5: All required sections are present and your writing is mostly fluent — good. However, the report uses no figures, tables or visual elements at all; adding even one table (e.g., stakeholders vs impacts) or figure would lift this criterion. Fix typos ('DICUSSION', inconsistent 'EACE' naming) and make your IEEE referencing consistent and complete.
